newsitem.title: FRANCE: French supreme Court sleaze ruling starts row.
newsitem.headline: French supreme Court sleaze ruling starts row.

text.p: French magistrates disputed on Friday whether the Supreme Court had made it easier for business to bribe politicians in a double-edged ruling on a high-profile sleaze case.
In Thursday's ruling on the case of former Lyon mayor Michel Noir, the Cour de Cassation refused to shorten the time limit for prosecuting the offence of receiving misused company funds.

However in a related case, it raised the possibility of narrowing the definition of "misuse of corporate funds", the basis for numerous recent prosecutions involving businessmen paying off politicians or their parties to win public contracts.

The court upheld an appeal by businessman Serge Crasnianski against conviction for bribing a relative of Noir to have the politician intervene to reduce his company's debt to the state, and ordered a retrial.
Crasnianski's lawyer had argued that while the bribe was illicit, his client had not acted for personal gain but in the interests of his company.

The lawyer said an act could not be regarded as contrary to corporate interest solely because it was illicit. "There is no misuse of corporate funds...if the company executive acted according to corporate interests," he said.
In ordering a retrial, the Supreme Court said a lower court had failed to give adequate grounds for convicting Crasnianski.

The court earlier rejected appeals by Noir, Cannes mayor Michel Mouillot and television newscaster Patrick Poivre d'Arvor against suspended prison sentences for receiving the proceeds of misused corporate funds in the 1980s.

Rejecting their argument that they could only be prosecuted within three years of the offence being committed, the court said the the three-year countdown started only from the moment the offence was uncovered.
A stricter interpretation of the statute of limitations could have closed dozens of corruption and party funding probes against politicians and senior businessmen.

Justice sources said several investigating magistrates had been awaiting the Supreme Court ruling to pursue a host of investigations targeting the ruling centre-right coalition parties as well as the opposition Socialists and Communists.
Magistrates disagreed on the consequences of the Crasnianski ruling, while politicians and business generally welcomed it.
The government has wanted to limit the definition of misuse of corporate funds which carries a maximum five-year jail term and fines of up to 2.5 million francs ($500,000).
The left-leaning Magistrates Union said the ruling could in effect make businessmen immune from prosecution for corruption.

In most recent sleaze scandals, businessmen were charged with misusing corporate funds in paying kickbacks. Politicians were accused of receiving the proceeds whether for themselves or for their party.
The rival centre-right United Magistrates Union said the ruling was no legal upheaval.
There was no indication the Supreme Court would extend its reasoning to cases of businessmen bribing officials in order to win public works contracts, it said.

Legal sources cited the case of former Genoble mayor Alain Carignon who was jailed for four years last year for accepting gifts from a water company in return for the city's water distribution contract.

Under the Supreme Court ruling, they argued, Carignon's conviction for being an accomplice to misuse of corporate funds could be quashed if the water company's executives could prove they had acted in the firm's interests.
